summary: The RSVP-TE SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object carries a Flags field of eight bits for options and attributes of an MPLS Label Switched Path, which is running out of room. This document defines a way to encode further attributes. It is standards-track and was replaced by RFC 5420.

eli5.summary: A form had only eight checkboxes and ran out. This adds a way to attach more options to a label-switched path.

questions: what is the lsp attributes object
subtitle: Extensible attribute encoding for MPLS label-switched paths

tldr.problem: The RSVP-TE signaling protocol uses an 8-bit Flags field in the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object to indicate options for label-switched paths, but all eight bits were nearly assigned and could not accommodate new attributes needed by future protocols.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines two new RSVP-TE objects—LSP_ATTRIBUTES and LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES—that carry attributes as TLVs (Type-Length-Value structures), allowing unlimited future attribute extension. It also defines an RRO Attributes Subobject to record which attributes were applied at each hop.
tldr.outcome: This mechanism became the standard way to extend MPLS signaling attributes going forward. RFC 5420 obsoleted this RFC to update the design, but the core concept of TLV-based attribute encoding persists.

today: RFC 4420 is a Proposed Standard defined in February 2006. It was obsoleted by RFC 5420 in February 2009, which refined the design and introduced new attribute mechanisms. However, the basic concept of using TLV-based attribute encoding in RSVP-TE messages remains the standard approach for extending MPLS signaling.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MPLS label-switched paths (LSPs) are set up using RSVP-TE, a signaling protocol based on the RSVP framework. The RSVP Path message includes a SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object that carries a Flags field with eight bits to indicate options and attributes of an LSP. Three of these bits were assigned in RFC 3209, two more in RFC 4090 for fast reroute, leaving only three bits available for new features. As new protocols and extensions were proposed, demand for those remaining bits threatened to exhaust the available space with no clear path for future expansion.

This document solves the problem by introducing new objects that can carry an unlimited number of attributes using a flexible TLV (Type-Length-Value) encoding scheme, while remaining backward compatible with routers that do not understand the new objects.
sections.eli5: The original form only had eight boxes. Designers needed a new form with many more boxes, but they had to make sure routers that do not understand the new form still work.

sections.title: Two Objects for Two Purposes
sections.content:
This RFC defines two new RSVP-TE message objects to carry attributes. The LSP_ATTRIBUTES object (class 197) carries attributes that do not need to be understood by every router along the path. Routers that do not recognize this object pass it through transparently, unchanged. This allows new attributes to be deployed across legacy networks without requiring upgrades to routers in the middle of the path.

The LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES object (class 67) carries attributes that every router must understand. If a router does not recognize this object or an attribute within it, it rejects the path setup with an error message. This ensures that critical attributes are always acted upon.

Both objects contain one or more Attributes TLVs. Currently, the RFC defines only the Attributes Flags TLV, which is an array of 32-bit words where each bit can represent a different attribute. New TLV types can be defined in the future for more complex attributes without changing the basic structure.
sections.eli5: The first form is passed along silently if routers do not understand it. The second form stops everything if a router does not understand it. That way, routers can work with both new and old equipment.

sections.title: Recording What Was Actually Applied
sections.content:
When a Path message with LSP attributes is sent through the network, each router may apply those attributes differently or report whether it supports them. The RFC introduces an RRO Attributes Subobject that routers push into the RECORD_ROUTE object (RRO) as they forward the Path message. This subobject carries the same Attributes Flags as the Attributes Flags TLV and is placed immediately before the IP address or link identifier of the router that is reporting it.

By examining the RRO Attributes subobjects in the Resv (reservation) message sent back, the ingress router can determine which attributes each hop successfully applied and which hops did not support the requested attributes. This allows operators to troubleshoot attribute support across the network.
sections.eli5: As the path goes through each router, each one writes down which features it actually used. The ingress router reads these notes to learn which routers did what.

sections.title: How to Use It: Three Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC provides guidance for three common deployment scenarios. For attributes that only the egress router must understand, use LSP_ATTRIBUTES: transit routers will pass it through transparently, and it reaches the destination unchanged. The egress router examines it and may report its compliance using the RRO Attributes subobject.

For attributes that certain key transit routers (such as area border routers or autonomous system border routers) must understand, again use LSP_ATTRIBUTES. These routers examine it and either act on it or pass it through; the ingress router learns what happened from the RRO.

For attributes that all routers on the path must support, use LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES. Any router that does not understand the object or an attribute within it rejects the path setup, ensuring that the attribute is honored everywhere or the path is not established.
sections.eli5: If only the destination needs to know, use the gentle form. If some routers in the middle must know, still use the gentle form. If every single router must know, use the strict form that stops everything if they do not understand.

sections.title: Extensibility Through IANA Management
sections.content:
This RFC lays out how future attributes will be registered and managed. The IANA maintains a registry of Attributes Flags bit numbers, with each bit tracked by its defining RFC, name, and which of three places it may be used: the Attributes Flags TLV on a Path message, the Attributes Flags TLV on a Resv message, or the RRO Attributes subobject. Future RFCs that define new bit values must specify in which contexts each bit has meaning.

Similarly, the IANA maintains a registry of new TLV type values so that future documents can define complex attributes beyond simple bit flags. This two-level extensibility scheme allows the protocol to grow without limit while keeping the base mechanism simple and implementable in small code.
sections.eli5: There is a public list of which bits mean what. New features are registered there so everyone knows what each number means.
